meta.titre: Sound: pitch, loudness, echo and resonance

sections.contenu_markdown: During a football match in a stadium in Garoua, the crowd's roar can be heard far away, and a vuvuzela produces a note so high it is easy to pick out. Shout in a quiet valley near Dschang and your own voice comes back a moment later. All of these are sound. The GCE O/L tests the nature of sound, the difference between pitch and loudness, echoes and resonance, so a clear grasp of the vocabulary is worth many marks.

items: A wave transfers energy without transferring matter, and its frequency is measured in hertz (Hz).
The speed, frequency and wavelength of a wave are related by $v = f\lambda$.
The speed of sound in air is taken as $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$.

sections.titre: The nature and properties of sound
sections.contenu_markdown:
**Sound** is produced by a vibrating object. It travels as a **longitudinal wave** of compressions (regions of high pressure) and rarefactions (regions of low pressure). It needs a material medium (solid, liquid or gas) and cannot travel through a vacuum.

| Property of the sound | Depends on | Heard as |
|---|---|---|
| Frequency $f$ | number of vibrations per second | **pitch** (high frequency = high note) |
| Amplitude | size of the vibration | **loudness** (larger amplitude = louder sound) |
| Waveform | mixture of frequencies | **quality** (timbre), which tells a flute from a guitar |

The audible range of a normal human ear is about $20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Sound above $20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$ is **ultrasound**. Changing the medium changes the speed and the wavelength of a sound but not its frequency, and $v = f\lambda$ always holds.

**Echo.** An echo is the reflection of sound by a hard, flat surface. The ear separates two sounds only if they are at least about $0.1\ \mathrm{s}$ apart, so the reflecting surface must be at least about $17\ \mathrm{m}$ away to hear a distinct echo. Echoes are used in sonar and in ultrasound scanning.

**Resonance.** Resonance occurs when an object is forced to vibrate by a source whose frequency equals the natural frequency of the object; the object then vibrates with a large amplitude. Examples: a tuning fork over a column of air of the right length, a swing pushed at the right rhythm, a glass shattering by a loud note of its own frequency.

variantes.nom: Reading a trace on an oscilloscope
variantes.quand_utiliser: When two sounds are displayed on a screen with the same time scale.
variantes.contenu_markdown: More waves across the same screen width means a **higher frequency** and a higher pitch. A taller trace (larger peak height) means a larger **amplitude** and a louder sound. The wavelength in air is found from $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f}$.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question asks for examples, demonstrations or effects of resonance.
variantes.contenu_markdown: To demonstrate resonance, hang several pendulums of different lengths from a stretched string and swing a heavy pendulum: the one of the same length vibrates with the greatest amplitude. Resonance helps radio tuning and musical instruments, but it can be destructive: soldiers break step on bridges so that the rhythm of marching does not match the bridge's natural frequency.

sections.enonce_markdown: A tuning fork produces a note of frequency $440\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in air, where the speed of sound is $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Calculate the period and the wavelength. (b) A second fork vibrates at twice this frequency. Compare its pitch and its wavelength with those of the first fork. (c) The first fork is now struck harder. State what changes and what stays the same.

etapes.justification: The period is the time for one vibration, $T = \dfrac{1}{f}$.
Doubling the frequency doubles the pitch (one octave higher), and the wavelength is halved because $v$ is fixed.

etapes.action: Describe the effect of striking harder.
etapes.justification: A harder strike gives a larger amplitude of vibration, but the natural frequency of the fork does not change.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The sound is louder (greater amplitude), the pitch (frequency $440\ \mathrm{Hz}$) and the wavelength are unchanged.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The first note has a period of **2.27 ms** and a wavelength of **0.75 m**. The second note has a **higher pitch** and a wavelength of **0.375 m**. Striking harder makes the sound **louder** without changing its pitch.

items.erreur_markdown: A student says that sound travels fastest in a vacuum because nothing gets in its way.
items.pourquoi_faux: Sound is a mechanical wave and needs particles to vibrate. It cannot travel through a vacuum.
items.correction_markdown: State that sound requires a material medium: solid, liquid or gas.

items.erreur_markdown: A student writes that a louder sound has a higher pitch.
items.pourquoi_faux: Loudness depends on amplitude. Pitch depends on frequency. A loud sound can be low-pitched.
items.correction_markdown: Link loudness to amplitude and pitch to frequency.

items.erreur_markdown: A student describes sound as a transverse wave.
items.pourquoi_faux: In sound the particles vibrate along the direction in which the wave travels, so it is longitudinal.
items.correction_markdown: Say that sound is a longitudinal wave of compressions and rarefactions.

items.erreur_markdown: A student thinks that an echo and resonance are the same effect because both make the sound heard again.
items.pourquoi_faux: An echo is reflection of sound by a surface. Resonance is a large-amplitude vibration produced when a driving frequency equals the natural frequency of an object.
items.correction_markdown: Use the word reflection for an echo, and natural frequency for resonance.

items.erreur_markdown: A student says that the frequency of a sound changes when it passes from air into water.
items.pourquoi_faux: The frequency is fixed by the source. The speed and the wavelength change in the new medium.
items.correction_markdown: Keep $f$ constant and use $\lambda = v/f$ with the new speed.

items.enonce_markdown: A bat emits a squeak of frequency $60\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$. Take the speed of sound in air as $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. (a) Can a normal human ear hear it? Explain. (b) Calculate the wavelength of the squeak in air.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The audible range is about $20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$. The squeak is at $60\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$, above $20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$, so it is **ultrasound** and cannot be heard.

(b) $\lambda = \dfrac{v}{f} = \dfrac{330}{60\,000} = 0.0055\ \mathrm{m}$. **Wavelength = 0.0055 m (5.5 mm).**

items.enonce_markdown: Two sounds, A and B, are shown on an oscilloscope with the same time-base setting. Over the same width of screen, trace A has $4$ complete waves with a peak height of $2$ divisions, and trace B has $8$ complete waves with a peak height of $1$ division. (a) Which sound has the higher pitch? (b) Which sound is louder? (c) If A has a frequency of $250\ \mathrm{Hz}$, find the frequency of B.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) B has more waves in the same time, so it has the higher frequency and **higher pitch**.

(b) A has the larger peak height, so a larger amplitude: **A is louder**.

(c) The frequency is proportional to the number of waves in the same time: $f_B = 250 \times \dfrac{8}{4} = 500\ \mathrm{Hz}$. **Frequency of B = 500 Hz.**

items.enonce_markdown: A note of frequency $660\ \mathrm{Hz}$ travels from air, where the speed of sound is $330\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, into sea water, where the speed is $1500\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Calculate (a) the wavelength in air, (b) the frequency in water and (c) the wavelength in water. (d) A hunter shouts in front of a cliff and hears no echo, although the cliff is smooth and hard. Suggest a reason.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\lambda_{\text{air}} = \dfrac{330}{660} = 0.50\ \mathrm{m}$.

(b) The frequency is set by the source and does not change: **660 Hz**.

(c) $\lambda_{\text{water}} = \dfrac{1500}{660} = 2.27\ \mathrm{m}$.

(d) For a distinct echo the surface must be at least about $17\ \mathrm{m}$ away; if the hunter stands closer, the echo arrives in less than $0.1\ \mathrm{s}$ and merges with the original shout.

**Wavelength in air = 0.50 m; frequency in water = 660 Hz; wavelength in water = 2.27 m.**

items_markdown: Sound is a longitudinal wave from a vibrating source; it needs a material medium and cannot travel in a vacuum.
Pitch depends on frequency; loudness depends on amplitude; quality depends on the waveform.
Audible range is about $20\ \mathrm{Hz}$ to $20\,000\ \mathrm{Hz}$; $v = f\lambda$, and only $v$ and $\lambda$ change from one medium to another.
An echo is a reflection of sound; the surface must be at least about 17 m away for a distinct echo.
Resonance happens when the driving frequency equals the natural frequency of an object, producing a large amplitude.
